questions.explanation: Congress gave the Fed two goals: maximum employment and stable prices (plus moderate long-term rates, which follow from the first two).

questions.text: The Fed's 2% inflation target is measured with which index?
questions.explanation: The Fed targets 2% on the PCE price index, and watches core PCE (ex food and energy) for the underlying trend.

questions.text: The idea that lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation is the…
questions.explanation: The Phillips curve: a tight labour market pushes up wages and prices — the reason the two mandates are linked.

questions.text: Payrolls +350k vs +150k expected. Inflation in line. The Fed most likely leans…
questions.explanation: A hot labour market means less need to support jobs and more risk of wage-driven inflation — a hawkish signal.

questions.text: Core PCE beats expectations for a 3rd straight month; jobs steady. Markets will price…
questions.explanation: Sticky inflation with a healthy job market points the Fed toward holding or hiking, so cut expectations get priced out.

questions.text: Unemployment jumps AND inflation falls below 2%. Both mandates point to…
questions.explanation: Weak jobs and below-target inflation both call for easier policy — the easy case where the mandates agree.

questions.text: Jobs data weaker than expected, inflation stronger than expected. For the Fed this means…
questions.explanation: Weak jobs argue for cuts, hot inflation for hikes — a stagflation-style trade-off with no painless option.

questions.text: In that conflict, if inflation expectations start rising, the Fed usually prioritises…
questions.explanation: Unanchored expectations can make inflation self-fulfilling, so the Fed tends to protect price stability first (the Volcker lesson).

questions.text: Payrolls badly miss; inflation in line. The 2-year Treasury yield most likely…
questions.explanation: The 2-year tracks expected Fed policy: weaker jobs → more expected cuts → lower 2-year yield.

questions.text: Unemployment rises because many more people started looking for work. Versus a rise from layoffs, this is…
questions.explanation: Rising participation means more labour supply, not falling demand — like Sept 2026, when the jobless rate rose to 4.2% as the labour force grew 485k.
